native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among Black men in this NLSY-79 cohort, incarceration is associated with a large, persistent wealth deficit whose dollar size scales with pre-jail economic position while its relative size is roughly constant. "Income level" is proxied by baseline composite_wealth_1985 because the file contains no income, earnings, wage or employment variable, grouped into rank tertiles. Of 1,465 Black men, the 143 ever jailed 1985-1994 gained only $4,601 in composite wealth from 1985 to 1996 versus $44,127 for the never-jailed (gap -$39,526; bootstrap 95% CI -$53,072 to -$27,724) and held $11,164 versus $55,544 in composite_wealth_1996 (gap -$44,380; CI -$57,251 to -$32,652), with 63.6% versus 37.7% holding zero-or-negative assets. Relative to baseline wealth the penalty is uniform: ever jailed raises the risk of ending with no positive assets by 23.8 percentage points (95% CI 15.7-32.0; OR 2.92, CI 2.00-4.26) and drops a man 14.5 percentile points down the 1996 wealth distribution (p=5e-13), with no moderation on the relative scale (asinh interaction p=0.37; odds-ratio interaction p=0.63). In nominal dollars the gap widens monotonically with 1985 wealth: -$11.5k in the bottom tertile, -$33.1k in the middle, -$85.7k in the top tertile of 1996 wealth (ever_jailed x stratum F=7.92, p=0.0004; tail-robust winsorised gaps -$10.7k, -$22.8k, -$63.7k with permutation p=0.17, 0.011, <0.001). Jail therefore appears to destroy accumulated, otherwise transferable assets rather than merely depressing a negligible stock: at the bottom of the income distribution the deficit is compressed toward zero dollars because even non-jailed Black men accumulated almost nothing (median 1996 wealth $0 in both groups), whereas among the third who entered the jail window with the most resources it is associated with roughly $60k-$86k less nominal wealth (median -$22,900) and a doubling of the share left with no assets (44% versus 20%). This is an association, not a causal estimate: the ever-jailed were already 43% poorer in 1985 ($6,564 vs $11,417), no covariates or jail timing/duration exist in the file, and within-stratum raw-mean permutation tests are non-significant after Holm (p=0.34-0.53) because a few multi-million-dollar observations dominate cell means; the robust signals are the distributional and assetlessness results.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Audit (12,013x6; zero missingness; 289 ever jailed = 2.41%; 1,899 exact duplicate rows; 37.97% of composite_wealth_1996 exactly zero; confirmed no income/earnings field). 2) Primary sample Black men (n=1,465; 143 jailed); co-primary outcomes = change in composite wealth 1985->1996 and 1996 level, always with means AND medians. 3) Income proxy = composite_wealth_1985 in rank-based tertiles with a seeded random tie-break (value-based quantiles collapse since ~40% of values tie at <=0); quartiles and a demoted 1990-wealth stratifier as robustness. 4) Within-stratum jailed-vs-not contrasts: means/medians/percentages, stratified bootstrap CIs (2,000), two-sided label permutation tests (10,000), Mann-Whitney, plus Hodges-Lehmann shifts, probability of superiority and 1%/99% winsorised means for tail robustness. 5) Effect modification: ever_jailed x stratum on the dollar scale (OLS on the 1985->1996 change, HC3; joint F test and linear-in-stratum trend) and on the asinh/rank scale (asinh(wealth/1000) adjusted for rank of 1985 wealth; percentile-rank regression), plus P(wealth<=0 in 1996) by logit and linear probability. 6) Holm correction within the 6-test primary family. 7) White men, Hispanic men and pooled Black respondents run identically as labelled comparison groups only. 8) Sensitivity: deduplicated rows, quartile strata, 1990 strata, winsorised means.

sub_hypo.text: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
sub_hypo.context: Black individuals in the National Longitudinal Study of Youth's 1979 cohort.
sub_hypo.relations: Incarceration may have a smaller negative impact on wealth for the high-income group than for those at lower wealth ranges.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.

sub_hypo.text: Among Black men in the NLSY-79 cohort, ever being jailed during 1985–1994 is associated with substantially lower wealth accumulation from 1985 to 1996 and lower wealth in 1996.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY-79 respondents (n=1,465), comparing 143 ever jailed during 1985–1994 with those never jailed during that period.
sub_hypo.relations: Mean 1985–1996 wealth gains are $4,601 versus $44,127 (jailed-minus-never-jailed gap −$39,526; bootstrap 95% CI −$53,072 to −$27,724). Mean 1996 wealth is $11,164 versus $55,544 (gap −$44,380; CI −$57,251 to −$32,652). These are associations, not causal estimates.

sub_hypo.text: The nominal-dollar wealth deficit associated with incarceration increases with baseline economic position.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY-79 respondents grouped into rank-based tertiles of composite_wealth_1985 with seeded random tie-breaking. Baseline wealth proxies income level because no income, earnings, wage or employment variable is available.
sub_hypo.relations: Jailed-minus-never-jailed 1996 wealth gaps widen from −$11.5k in the bottom baseline-wealth tertile to −$33.1k in the middle and −$85.7k in the top. The incarceration-by-stratum dollar-scale interaction for 1985–1996 wealth change has F=7.92, p=0.0004. Winsorised gaps are −$10.7k, −$22.8k and −$63.7k (permutation p=0.17, 0.011 and <0.001). Within-stratum raw-mean permutation tests are not significant after Holm correction (p=0.34–0.53), reflecting sensitivity to extreme wealth observations.

sub_hypo.text: The relative wealth disadvantage associated with incarceration is roughly uniform across baseline economic positions.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY-79 respondents, assessing relative-scale effect modification by baseline 1985 wealth using asinh, percentile-rank and assetlessness models.
sub_hypo.relations: Ever being jailed is associated with a 14.5-percentile-point lower position in the 1996 wealth distribution (p=5e-13). There is no statistically significant moderation on the relative scale: asinh interaction p=0.37 and odds-ratio interaction p=0.63.

sub_hypo.text: Incarceration is associated with a higher probability of having zero or negative wealth in 1996.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY-79 respondents, comparing ever jailed during 1985–1994 with never jailed, including models accounting for baseline wealth.
sub_hypo.relations: Zero-or-negative 1996 wealth occurs in 63.6% of ever-jailed men versus 37.7% of never-jailed men. Relative to baseline wealth, the estimated increase is 23.8 percentage points (95% CI 15.7–32.0), with OR 2.92 (CI 2.00–4.26).

sub_hypo.text: The incarceration-associated dollar deficit is compressed at the bottom of the baseline wealth distribution but substantial among men who initially held the most resources.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY-79 respondents in the bottom and top rank-based tertiles of 1985 composite wealth.
sub_hypo.relations: In the bottom tertile, median 1996 wealth is $0 for both incarceration groups. In the top tertile, incarceration is associated with roughly $60k–$86k less nominal wealth, a median gap of −$22,900, and approximately twice the proportion with no positive assets (44% versus 20%). This pattern is interpreted as consistent with loss of accumulated assets, not as causal evidence.

sub_hypo.text: Men classified as ever jailed during 1985–1994 already had lower wealth in 1985, limiting causal interpretation of subsequent wealth differences.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY-79 respondents; the file contains no additional covariates or incarceration timing or duration information.
sub_hypo.relations: Mean baseline wealth is $6,564 for ever-jailed men versus $11,417 for never-jailed men, approximately 43% lower.
